02 / Case study: SmartSuit (in progress)

SmartSuit: a flotation shirt kids can wear every day.

Senior design project, team of five, Purdue School of Mechanical Engineering. Critical Design Review submitted October 2026; results below are analysis, not yet pool-tested.

01

Problem and requirements

Drowning is the leading cause of death for children ages 1 to 4, and children with autism face added risk. The goal is a scalable, everyday-wearable shirt that is sensory-friendly, tamperproof, and alerts a guardian when it is submerged. It must give 60 N of buoyancy, hold 50 N for 6 hours, turn the child face-up, and stay at or below 5 psi.

02

Constraints and stakeholders

The device must output 60N of buoyant force to align with the international life jacket standards (UL 12402). Purdue safety requirements limit bladder gauge pressure to 5 psi. The device must be fully functional up to 2m of depth and remain inflated for 6h while tilting the child on their back.

03

Design and analysis

Buoyancy and the ideal gas law sized the bladder at 7.0 L, which gives 68.7 N at 3.98 psi. It is split into a 4.46 L chest, a 1.34 L back and a 1.2 L neck pillow so the child rolls face-up. An FMEA flagged nine failure modes above an RPN of 200, mostly bladder leaks, which drove the heat-welded seams for the bladder, the lower pressure and the removable bladder.

04

Actuation and electronics

A UML MK5 cartridge and valve inflates the bladder on water contact. A Hall sensor wakes a Seeed XIAO ESP32S3, which sends an LTE-M alert through an M5Stack CatM module while three white LEDs flash as a survivor light. Power is a 400 mAh LiPo battery with a 2 A slow-blow fuse.

05

Status and next steps

Next: Manufacture the design and integrate the electronic package. Test all above mentioned sub styems and validate them against existing benchmarks and engineering requirements

02 / Case study: H2 Test Cell

H2 Test Cell Implementation: getting an engine test cell ready for hydrogen.

Research project at Purdue University. This follows my research poster on the preparation phase: nitrogen purging, fuel monitoring and electrical safety.

01

Problem and goal

Vehicle emissions from diesel and gasoline engines made up 29% of US carbon emissions in 2022. Hydrogen combustion has no carbon emissions, so the project aims to convert an existing engine to run on hydrogen. This phase prepares the test cell to handle hydrogen fuel safely.

02

Nitrogen cleansing system

The pipe routing already existed, but the parts that move nitrogen to actuate valves and purge the system did not. Four elements were selected: a changeover, a regulator, a caddy for the outdoor tanks, and oxygen-cleaned hoses sized to the 0.25 in outputs.

03

Fuel monitoring

Test-cell engines are very sensitive, so fuel pressure has to stay constant and be watched closely. A bracket attaches the sensors to the fuel supply, and double block and bleed valves control the flow and relieve pressure. The valves are driven by solenoids powered by compressed nitrogen.

04

Electrical components

Relay logic governs the engine safety system and is monitored from the control room. Hydrogen adds safety requirements, so the existing relay setup has to be considerably expanded. A fusible valve shuts off fuel when the temperature gets too high, and a hydrogen sensor detects leaks.

05

Status and next steps

The sensor code is planned for the following summer semester. The relay logic still needs to be expanded and connected to the data processing system, and the hydrogen sensor has to be calibrated to the desired H2 emissions.

02 / Case study: Gearbox

Go-Kart Gearbox: sizing a 20:1 reduction.

ME 354 course project, solo, April 2026. Every gear, key, bearing and shaft diameter was sized and checked in MATLAB against a minimum safety factor of 1 at 99% reliability.

01

Problem and requirements

Design the smallest gearbox that steps 10,000 rpm down to 500 rpm at a constant 50 hp, linking a go-kart engine to the wheels. The input and output shafts were given; the gears, intermediate shaft, keys and bearings were mine to select and design.

02

Constraints and concepts

Standard 20° full-depth gears and AISI 1045 throughout, medium drive fits, 1 mm fillets. Gears were designed for 1 million cycles, bearings for 10 million, and the shaft for infinite life. Two ratio splits (4 × 5 and 5 × 4) were checked at modules 1.5 to 3.

03

Design and analysis

AGMA bending and contact stress sized the gears. The pinion on the intermediate shaft needed 40 teeth to reach a safety factor of 1, which only worked with a 4:1 first stage, giving 16, 64, 40 and 200 teeth at module 3. Keys were checked in shear, bearings from a force balance, and the shaft with the Goodman criterion at the keyway.

04

Components and drawings

Gears came from the Misumi catalog and bearings from the Timken catalog. Gear 4, the shaft and the keys are custom. The parts are documented in dimensioned Siemens NX drawings.

05

Outcome and next steps

The shaft had to grow from 11 mm to 35 mm to pass fatigue, ending at a safety factor of 1.1. Still to address: the constant-speed assumption, vibration from rough roads (no suspension), the input and output shaft connections, and real-world testing.

02 / Case study: Air engine

Single-Cylinder Air Engine: a full assembly in NX.

Team CAD project, December 2023. Modeled in Siemens NX to ASME standards.

01

Goal

Build a complete CAD model of a single-cylinder air engine, with every part modeled individually and then assembled. The design must be fully constrained and must include a complication

02

Tools and standards

Each part was drawn in Siemens NX following ASME standards, so the models and drawings share one dimensioning convention.

03

Assembly

The parts were mated into a single assembly. The exploded view shows how the base plate, upright supports, disc, shafts, bevel gears, spring and countersunk screws fit together. All elements were constraint properly so that the engine could function properly in the model. 

04

Complexity

Bevel gear system was created to generate vertical motion. Output shaft was split in two sections, and both sections were linked with bevel gears found on McMaster.

05

Outcome

The result is a complete assembly with an exploded view that documents every part of the engine and functions properly.

02 / Case study: MACRO rover

MACRO: a Mars cargo rover prototype that follows a line, climbs and drops cargo.

Team design project, team of four, December 2023. The prototype was built from the parts provided and programmed to run a course on its own.

01

Problem and requirements

Build a prototype Mars Cargo Mobility System (MACRO) that follows a black line creating a path with forks, small obstacles and elevation changes with no human input, then carries cargo of different shapes and drops it upright within a 6 in radius of the correct magnetic beacon.

02

Mechanical design

The design went through three iterations. The first put heavy parts at the back and struggled on the hill, so the battery and Raspberry Pi moved forward to favor the driving wheels. The second twisted its plastic axles and its cargo track could not hold different shapes, so independent axels were used and the cargo was redesigned as a ramp. The final rover has drive motors side by side for a rigid frame, gears near the wheels, a passive ski at the rear that lifts the back wheels on a slope, and line sensors on pivots that tilt up the ramp.

03

Cargo system

A motorized folding ramp holds the cargo in a V-shaped cradle with side barriers and a drop-down cone holder, then opens to slide it out. The ramp motor is geared 5:1 to counterbalance the cargo weight.

04

Software

Two line-following methods: two-sensor center following for obstacles, and single-sensor edging to avoid forks. An IMU reads angle and magnetic field with a rolling average; a rise in angle triggers a 2-second speed boost to clear hills. A state-based program moves between obstacle, edging, magnetic and post-drop states, with motor encoders converting cm/s into degrees per second.

05

Outcome and lessons

The rover drove the full course without damage, cleared the elevation changes (the dowel rod took two attempts), and held its cargo securely. The magnet logic failed in the demo: the robot did not turn at the beacon, and the three drops landed 7.75 to 9.5 in away, outside the 6 in target. Magnets were also double-counted when the robot stopped over them. The team estimated the fix at three or four lines of code.
